warmup.q: Inside coroutineScope { }, three async calls ask three providers for a price. One provider throws IOException after 50 ms; the other two would answer at 120 and 300 ms. What does the quote request get?
options: The better of the two prices that came back, after 300 ms
The IOException after about 50 ms, and the other two calls are cancelled
The IOException after 300 ms, once the other two calls have finished
Two prices and a null for the provider that failed
warmup.why: A failed child cancels its parent at once, and a plain scope then cancels the other children and rethrows. So the request fails at 50 ms with the IOException, and the two calls that would have answered are cancelled. That is right when you need every answer and wrong when any one will do. The fix for a quote is supervisorScope, this lesson's first change.

sections.h: One request, three providers, one deadline
sections.html:
Lesson 1 left the server with a QuoteSource that must return a future at once. This lesson writes the source. For each request it asks Northbank, Eastgate and Fjord for a price, keeps the lowest, and answers within a deadline whatever the providers do. Lowest is what a customer buying the currency wants; a real dealing desk compares bid and ask, but the fan-out is the same either way.

The shape is the concurrent decomposition from "Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope": start all three calls, then wait for them. With latencies of 120, 300 and 200 ms, one call after another takes 620 ms. Started together they take 300 ms, the time of the slowest:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: Mono.zip subscribes to all three sources at once
Mono<List<Quote>> allPrices(String symbol) {
    return Mono.zip(northbank.quote(symbol), eastgate.quote(symbol), fjord.quote(symbol))
            .map(t -> List.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()));
}
Kotlin
suspend fun allPrices(symbol: String): List<Quote> = coroutineScope {
    providers.map { p -> async { p.quote(symbol) } }   // 1. start all three
        .awaitAll()                                     // 2. then wait: as long as the slowest
}

The deadline is the next decision. A price that arrives after 2 seconds is useless to a checkout page with a 300 ms budget. Give each call the deadline, start them together, and the whole request ends by the deadline:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: a timeout on each source, turned into "no answer"
Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) {
    return call.timeout(DEADLINE)
            .map(Optional::of)
            .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty()));
}
Kotlin
providers.map { p ->
    async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(symbol) } }   // null if p misses the deadline
}

withTimeoutOrNull is cancellation with a clock ("Cancellation and timeouts"). At the deadline it cancels the late call, which stops at its next suspension point, and returns null for it.

Why one deadline per call, and not one withTimeout around the whole fan-out? Both bound the request. Around the whole fan-out, the timeout cancels everything and throws away the answers that did arrive: Northbank answered at 120 ms and Fjord at 200 ms, and you would still have nothing to send. Per call, only the late provider drops out, as the figure shows. Because all the calls start together, a per-call deadline is also a deadline for the request.

sections.h: Let one provider fail alone, and tell your cancel from theirs
sections.html:
The first draft of BestQuote, the starting code of this lesson's lab, uses coroutineScope and withTimeout. Both are wrong for a quote, for reasons from earlier lessons.

coroutineScope treats its children as one unit of work. When Northbank throws IOException at 50 ms, the scope cancels Eastgate and Fjord and rethrows ("Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers"). That is right for a payment details page that needs all three answers. A quote needs any one of them. supervisorScope lets each child fail alone: a failed async keeps its exception in its Deferred, and await hands it to you, where you turn it into "no answer".

withTimeout signals a late call with TimeoutCancellationException, and that is a CancellationException. The usual rule, rethrow CancellationException so a cancel is never swallowed, now bites: one provider's timeout looks like a cancel of the whole request, and ends it. withTimeoutOrNull turns your own deadline into a plain null. But a provider can still throw TimeoutCancellationException from deep inside its own HTTP client, and this section's demo has one that does. So be precise and rethrow only when your coroutine was cancelled. ensureActive() makes exactly that check:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: each source handles its own error, so the zip never sees one
Mono<Optional<Quote>> alone(Mono<Quote> call) {
    return call.map(Optional::of)
            .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty()))   // a failure stays with its provider
            .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty());                 // and so does an empty answer
}
Kotlin
private suspend fun Deferred<Quote?>.awaitOrNull(): Quote? =
    try {
        await()
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()   // we were cancelled ourselves: this rethrows
        null                                        // only the provider's call ended that way
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        null                                        // the provider failed: no answer from it
    }

If the request itself was cancelled (the client hung up), ensureActive() throws and the cancel carries on up. If it returns, the cancellation belonged to the provider's call, and that provider simply has no answer. The demo runs the same three calls in three scopes:

Scope Outcome
coroutineScope, awaitAll fails at 50 ms: IOException: northbank 503
supervisorScope, rethrow every cancel fails at 100 ms: TimeoutCancellationException
supervisorScope, rethrow only our cancel eastgate 1.0841 at 300 ms

Reactor has no such trap, because cancellation there is not an error signal: you isolate each source with onErrorResume before Mono.zip. The compare block below puts the two whole fan-outs side by side.

Run it. Then, in callAll(), move async { fjord() } to the end of the list and predict the second line again.

= try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { null } private suspend fun Deferred<String>.careful(): String? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(); null } catch (e: Exception) { null } private suspend fun TestScope.attempt(what: String, block: suspend () -> List<String?>) { val t0 = currentTime val outcome = try { "answers ${block()}" } catch (e: Exception) { "failed: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" of ")}" } println("%-40s at %3d ms %s".format(what, currentTime - t0, outcome)) } /** The same three calls in three scopes: who survives a failure, and who survives a timeout? The careful one answers [null, null, eastgate 1.0841] at 300 ms. With Fjord last, the naive version waits for Eastgate first, then rethrows Fjord's exception: it fails at 300 ms instead of 100, and still throws away Eastgate's price. The Java twin shows the Reactor side: the raw Mono.zip fails on Northbank's error, and with onErrorResume on each call it answers with Eastgate at about 300 ms.

sections.h: When nobody answers, serve the last good quote and say it is stale
sections.html:
Sometimes all three providers miss the deadline: a network partition, or the minutes after a market opens. The service then has three options. It can wait longer, fail the request, or serve the last price it saw. Waiting longer breaks the deadline, which is the one promise the service makes. Failing is honest, and useless to a checkout page that only needs an indicative price. So BestQuote keeps the last live quote per symbol and serves it marked stale, 7 STALE EURUSD 1.0841 eastgate, and the client decides whether stale is good enough.

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: an empty Optional switches to the cache
.flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(symbol)))
.doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); })   // only live answers refresh the cache
Kotlin
val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price }
if (best != null) {
    cache.remember(best)                       // only live answers refresh the cache
    return best
}
return cache.lastGood(symbol)?.asStale()       // stale beats nothing
    ?: throw NoQuoteException(symbol)          // the handler writes "7 ERR no quote for EURUSD"

Two rules keep the cache honest. Only live answers go into it: if a stale answer could refresh the cache, one old price could be served forever. And with nothing cached, the request fails with NoQuoteException, which lesson 1's handler turns into 7 ERR no quote for EURUSD. A production cache would also have an age limit, so that a price from three seconds ago is served and one from last night is not.

Check yourself: after an outage the providers recover, and on the next request Eastgate answers 1.0839 and Fjord 1.0842. What does the client get, and what does the cache hold for EURUSD afterwards? (OK EURUSD 1.0839 eastgate, and the cache now holds that live quote in place of the old one.)

sections.h: Bind each request to its connection with scope.future
sections.html:
Lesson 1's handler calls quote on the event loop, and it cancels the future when the client hangs up. QuoteService connects that future to a coroutine:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: toFuture() subscribes, and cancelling the future cancels the subscription
final class ReactorQuoteSource implements QuoteSource {
    @Override
    public CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String symbol) {
        return best(symbol).toFuture();                              // returns at once; cancel() reaches the zip
    }
}
Kotlin
class QuoteService(context: CoroutineContext, private val best: BestQuote) : QuoteSource, AutoCloseable {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(context + SupervisorJob())   // owned; failures stay per request

    override fun quote(symbol: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> =
        scope.future { best.quote(symbol) }                          // returns at once; cancel() reaches it

    override fun close() = scope.cancel()
}

scope.future { } starts a coroutine in the service's scope and returns a CompletableFuture at once, so the event loop never waits. The link works in both directions ("Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads"): when the coroutine finishes, the future completes, and when someone cancels the future, the coroutine is cancelled. The second direction is what binds a request to its connection. The client hangs up, channelInactive cancels the future, the future coroutine is cancelled, and the cancel travels down the job tree to the supervisorScope and its three provider calls ("Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree"). Each request is a small tree whose root is that coroutine, and the channel's lifetime bounds it.

Why not give each channel its own CoroutineScope and cancel it in channelInactive? That works too, and it is the shape to pick when the handler itself is written in Kotlin. Here the Java handler from lesson 1 already keeps every pending future and cancels them on close, so a scope per channel would track the same requests twice. With future { }, the Java side holds the handle, the Kotlin side holds the tree, and neither needs to know how the other works.

Two choices in the scope matter. The scope uses SupervisorJob. With a plain Job, one request that fails with NoQuoteException would cancel its parent, and with it every other request in flight; every later future would then come back cancelled at once. And the dispatcher is passed in. Production uses Dispatchers.Default. The tests pass a StandardTestDispatcher, so every delay and every deadline runs on virtual time, and a test that checks a 300 ms deadline takes a few milliseconds.

The Java twin of this section's demo shows what you'd lose with a plain CompletableFuture built from three supplyAsync calls: cancelling the outer future cancels 0 of the 3 calls, and all three answer later with nobody listening.

The client hangs up after 120 ms. */ fun main() { val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default + SupervisorJob()) // the service's scope val request = scope.future { // what QuoteService.quote returns supervisorScope { listOf("northbank" to 300L, "eastgate" to 400L, "fjord" to 500L) .map { (name, latency) -> async { call(name, latency) } }.awaitAll() } } Thread.sleep(120) println("client hangs up at ${ms()} ms: the handler calls request.cancel(true)") request.cancel(true) Thread.sleep(600) println("at ${ms()} ms: coroutines still running in the scope: ${scope.coroutineContext.job.children.count()}") scope.cancel() }

The client hangs up after 120 ms. */ public class HangUpDemoJava { static final long t0 = System.nanoTime(); static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } static String call(String name, long latency) { try { Thread.sleep(latency); System.out.println(" " + name + " answered at " + ms() + " ms, and nobody is listening"); return name; } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" " + name + " interrupted at " + ms() + " ms"); return null; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> calls = List.of( CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("northbank", 300), pool), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("eastgate", 400), pool), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("fjord", 500), pool)); CompletableFuture<List<String>> request = CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(v -> calls.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList()); Thread.sleep(120); System.out.println("client hangs up at " + ms() + " ms: the handler calls request.cancel(true)"); request.cancel(true); System.out.println("request cancelled: " + request.isCancelled() + ", calls cancelled: " + calls.stream().filter(CompletableFuture::isCancelled).count() + " of 3"); } // close() waits for the three calls, which finish anyway System.out.println("at " + ms() + " ms: all three calls have finished"); } }

try.expect: All three calls print cancelled a few milliseconds after the hang-up, and the scope has 0 coroutines left: the cancel went from the future to the coroutine and down to its children. The Java twin reports calls cancelled: 0 of 3, and the three providers answer at about 300, 400 and 500 ms with nobody listening. CompletableFuture.cancel completed the outer future and stopped nothing.

analogy: A dealer on an FX desk needs a price for a customer. She calls three banks at once on three phones and starts a kitchen timer. If one bank's line drops, she keeps listening to the other two; that is supervisorScope, where coroutineScope would hang up all three phones. When the timer rings she hangs up on whoever is still talking and quotes the best price she has. If nobody answered, she reads yesterday's price off the board with an "indicative" sticker on it. And if the customer walks away from the desk, she hangs up all three phones at once, which is the cancel travelling down the job tree. The analogy breaks at hanging up: a dealer's phone goes dead the instant she puts it down. A coroutine stops only at its next suspension point, so a provider client stuck in blocking IO keeps going until its call returns ("Cancellation and timeouts").
world: A checkout service fans out all the time: FX rates from several liquidity providers, a fraud score, merchant fees, a BIN lookup. Decide per call which scope it needs. Where any answer will do, as with several FX providers or several fraud vendors, use supervisorScope and a deadline per call. Where the response needs every answer, as with an account, its limits and its risk flags, use coroutineScope so that one failure cancels the rest at once. A Quarkus REST endpoint written as a Kotlin suspend fun runs on the event loop ("Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads"), so the fan-out inside it must suspend, never block. And keep the stale-price rule in mind for anything that moves money: an indicative price may be stale, but a price you book a payment at must be live and confirmed.
mistake: The most common mistake is building a best-of fan-out with coroutineScope and awaitAll(), then trying to rescue it with runCatching { deferred.await() } when one bad provider starts failing every quote. It doesn't work: in a plain scope, a failed child cancels its parent and siblings the moment it fails, long before your runCatching runs ("Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers"). The second version of the same mistake catches correctly but rethrows every CancellationException, and one provider's internal timeout then ends the request. Use supervisorScope, give each call withTimeoutOrNull, and in the catch rethrow only after currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() says the cancel was yours.

compare.title: The fan-out with Reactor's Mono.zip and with coroutines

java.title: BestQuoteReactor.java
java.html: // Reactor: errors, timeouts and empties become values at each source, then Mono.zip Mono<Quote> best(String symbol) { return Mono.zip(inTime(northbank.quote(symbol)), inTime(eastgate.quote(symbol)), inTime(fjord.quote(symbol))) .map(t -> Stream.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()) .flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.comparing(Quote::price))) .flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(symbol))) .doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); }); } Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.timeout(DEADLINE) .map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())) // a failure or a timeout: no answer .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()); // an empty source would empty the zip } Mono<Quote> fromCache(String symbol) { Quote last = cache.lastGood(symbol); return last != null ? Mono.just(last.asStale()) : Mono.error(new NoQuoteException(symbol)); }

kotlin.title: BestQuote.kt
kotlin.html: class BestQuote( private val providers: List<Provider>, private val deadline: Duration, private val cache: QuoteCache = QuoteCache(), ) { suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote { val answers = supervisorScope { // 1. a failed call doesn't cancel the others providers .map { p -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(symbol) } } } // 2. late is null, not an exception .map { it.awaitOrNull() } // 3. failed is null too }.filterNotNull() val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price } if (best != null) { cache.remember(best) return best } return cache.lastGood(symbol)?.asStale() ?: throw NoQuoteException(symbol) // 4. stale beats nothing } private suspend fun Deferred<Quote?>.awaitOrNull(): Quote? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() // we were cancelled ourselves: this rethrows null // only the provider's call ended that way: no answer } catch (e: Exception) { null // the provider failed: no answer from it } }

compare.note: Both start the three calls together, give each its own deadline, turn a failure into "no answer", keep the lowest price and fall back to the cache. In Reactor every outcome becomes a value at the source: a timeout is an error signal you resume from, and an empty source is a third outcome you must name with defaultIfEmpty, or Mono.zip completes empty ("Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest"). Nothing runs until something subscribes, and cancelling the subscription cancels the three calls. In Kotlin the same policy is ordinary control flow: a scope, try/catch, minByOrNull. The scope guarantees that when quote returns, every call is either done or cancelled. The price of that directness is the CancellationException rule, which only coroutines have: a timeout is a cancel, so you must tell your own cancel from a provider's.

worked.title: Test the deadline and the hang-up on virtual time

steps.say: Make the providers controllable on the test clock. delay inside runTest uses virtual time, so a fake that delays 1,000 ms costs nothing, and recording cancellations in the catch tells the test exactly who was stopped.
steps.code: class FakeProvider( override val name: String, private val price: String, private val latency: Duration, private val cancelled: MutableList<String>, ) : Provider { override suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote { try { delay(latency) // 1. virtual time under runTest } catch (e: CancellationException) { cancelled += name // 2. record who was cancelled throw e } return Quote.live(symbol, price, name) } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor: Mono.delay runs on Schedulers.parallel(), which virtual time replaces Mono<Quote> fake(String name, String price, Duration latency, List<String> cancelled) { return Mono.delay(latency) // 1. virtual time under StepVerifier .map(x -> Quote.live("EURUSD", price, name)) .doOnCancel(() -> cancelled.add(name)); // 2. record who was cancelled }

steps.say: Test the deadline. currentTime is the virtual clock, so the assertion can be exact: 300, not "under 400". A real-time version would take 300 ms per test and could fail on a busy build machine.
steps.code: @Test fun `a provider slower than the deadline is cancelled at the deadline`() = runTest { val best = BestQuote(listOf(northbank(120), eastgate(1_000), fjord(200)), deadline = 300.milliseconds) val quote = best.quote("EURUSD") assertThat(quote.provider).isEqualTo("fjord") assertThat(currentTime).isEqualTo(300) // 3. exact, and the test takes milliseconds assertThat(cancelled).containsExactly("eastgate") }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor: StepVerifier on virtual time StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> best("EURUSD")) // build the Mono inside the supplier .expectSubscription() .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofMillis(299)) .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // 3. exactly at the deadline .expectNextMatches(q -> q.provider().equals("fjord")) .verifyComplete(); assertThat(cancelled).containsExactly("eastgate");

steps.say: Test the hang-up through QuoteService. Pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) as its context: the service's own scope then runs on the test clock too. runCurrent() runs what is due now, without moving the clock.
steps.code: @Test fun `cancelling the future cancels all three provider calls`() = runTest { val service = QuoteService(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), slowBest) // 4. inject the test clock val future = service.quote("EURUSD") runCurrent() // the three calls have started future.cancel(true) // what channelInactive does runCurrent() assertThat(cancelled).containsExactlyInAnyOrder("northbank", "eastgate", "fjord") assertThat(service.inFlight).isEqualTo(0) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor: cancelling toFuture() cancels the subscription at once CompletableFuture<Quote> future = source.quote("EURUSD"); future.cancel(true); // what channelInactive does assertThat(cancelled).containsExactlyInAnyOrder("northbank", "eastgate", "fjord");

steps.say: Know where virtual time stops. A delay inside withContext(Dispatchers.Default) escapes the test scheduler and takes real time ("Shared state and testing coroutines"), which is why the service takes its dispatcher as a parameter. The two end-to-end tests in this lab use Dispatchers.Default and a real Netty server, so they assert only with latches: 6 provider calls started, 6 cancelled after the hang-up. Self-check: what would currentTime read in a test that built QuoteService(Dispatchers.Default, ...) inside runTest? (0: the coroutines ran on real threads, and the virtual clock never moved.)

lab.title: Fan out to three providers, and cancel on hang-up
steps: Run the tests. Ten of eleven fail. The Java files in l02 are lesson 1's solution, carried over; the tests' providers are in src/test/.../l02/FakeProvider.kt.
Fix BestQuote along points 1 to 3 of its KDoc: supervisorScope, withTimeoutOrNull inside each async, and an await that turns failures into null and rethrows only your own cancel.
Add point 4: remember the best live quote, else serve cache.lastGood(symbol)?.asStale(), else throw NoQuoteException(symbol). The six BestQuote tests should pass.
Write QuoteService: a private scope from context + SupervisorJob(), quote with scope.future { }, inFlight from the scope's job, and close.
Run the tests until all eleven pass, including the two over TCP. Run them once more.
hints: If the deadline test fails with TimeoutCancellationException: Timed out after 300ms of _virtual_ ... time, you still use withTimeout, or you rethrow every CancellationException.
supervisorScope returns what its block returns. Map the deferreds to awaitOrNull() inside the block, and filterNotNull() outside it.
scope.future { } is in kotlinx.coroutines.future. It starts the coroutine on the scope's dispatcher and returns the future at once.
inFlight is scope.coroutineContext.job.children.count(); job is an extension property from kotlinx.coroutines.
lab.done: All eleven tests in FanOutTest pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: Write the best-of fan-out from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write BestQuote.quote(symbol) from memory: all providers at once, the same deadline for each, a failed or late provider counts as no answer, your own cancel still propagates, the lowest price wins, and with no answer you serve the cached quote as stale or throw NoQuoteException. Which line would break the request when a provider's own client times out?

answer.html: suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote { val answers = supervisorScope { providers .map { p -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(symbol) } } } .map { d -> try { d.await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(); null } catch (e: Exception) { null } } }.filterNotNull() val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price } if (best != null) return best.also { cache.remember(it) } return cache.lastGood(symbol)?.asStale() ?: throw NoQuoteException(symbol) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor Mono<Quote> best(String symbol) { return Mono.zip(inTime(northbank.quote(symbol)), inTime(eastgate.quote(symbol)), inTime(fjord.quote(symbol))) .map(t -> Stream.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()).flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.comparing(Quote::price))) .flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(symbol))) .doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); }); } Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.timeout(DEADLINE).map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())) .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()); }

recap: Fan out with async inside a scope: three providers at 120, 300 and 200 ms answer in 300 ms instead of 620.
Give each call the deadline with withTimeoutOrNull. A late provider drops out as null and the others still count; one timeout around the whole fan-out throws away answers that already arrived.
supervisorScope lets each provider fail alone. coroutineScope cancels the other calls at the first failure, which is right only when you need every answer.
A provider's own timeout is a CancellationException too. In the catch, currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() rethrows only if your coroutine was cancelled.
With no answer, serve the last live quote marked STALE, or fail with NoQuoteException. Only live answers refresh the cache.

scope.future { } gives the Java handler a future at once, and cancelling it cancels the request's coroutine and its provider calls. The scope uses SupervisorJob, so one failed request can't cancel the others.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why BestQuote needs supervisorScope, withTimeoutOrNull on every call and that odd ensureActive() in a catch, and what actually stops the provider calls when a client hangs up. Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: A quote needs any one price, not all three, so one provider failing must not cancel the others. In a plain coroutineScope a failed child cancels its siblings at once, so we use supervisorScope, where each async keeps its failure for await and we turn it into no answer. Each call gets the deadline with withTimeoutOrNull: a late provider becomes null and the others still count, and since all calls start together the request ends by the deadline. withTimeout would be worse because its TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException, and a provider's own client can throw one too. If we rethrew every CancellationException, one provider's timeout would end the request. So in the catch we call ensureActive: it throws only if our own coroutine was cancelled, and otherwise that provider just has no answer. With no answers we serve the last live quote marked stale, or fail with NoQuoteException. On hang-up, lesson 1's handler cancels the future in channelInactive; scope.future links that future to the request's coroutine, so the coroutine is cancelled and the cancel goes down the job tree to the three provider calls. The service's scope uses SupervisorJob so one failed request can't cancel the rest.

deeper.html:
Four refinements a production fan-out often adds.

Propagate the deadline. The service knows that a request has, say, 180 ms left; the provider doesn't. Many RPC systems carry the remaining time in a header, so that the provider can give up too instead of finishing work nobody will read. With coroutines you compute it from a start time and pass it down; withTimeoutOrNull then wraps the remaining budget, not a fixed number.

Answer early when the answer can't improve. If the request only needs a price within 0.5 pip of the best seen in the last second, it can return as soon as one such price arrives and cancel the rest. That is select over the onAwait clauses ("Channels, select and pipelines"), with the losers cancelled by hand.

Put an age on the cache. Store the time with each quote and refuse to serve one older than a few seconds. Then a long outage ends in a clear error, not in a price from the morning.

Mind the await legacy rule. The kotlinx.coroutines KDoc notes that await() on a Deferred that someone else cancelled throws CancellationException in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. This lesson's ensureActive() check is the documented way to tell the two apart, and it is worth using anywhere you await work you didn't start.

Lesson 3 of this track adds what the fan-out still lacks: a limit on how many calls each provider sees at once, retries for the calls that are safe to repeat, a hedge for the slowest provider, and load shedding when the whole service is full.
